segments.t: Past five o'clock Friday afternoon, Chen stands behind the front desk with his small brass screwdriver while Qing and Manager Zhou watch him add something new to the wooden key board. Let's listen in first.
这块木板在我手里十五年，一直只有一到八号挂钩。
您看右边——清漆下面本来就有两个小小的螺丝孔。
不会吧！三十年前，九号挂钩就挂在那儿！
转一圈，转两圈……结实的黄铜九号挂钩，回家了。
老陈，我可以亲手把阳光房的大钥匙挂上去吗？
挂吧，小晴。这个星期你辛苦了。
等等——老陈，你账本里夹着的那张塑封卡片是什么？
哈！老陈，你偷偷留了一份我打印的咖啡馆菜单？！
只是因为你的大数字不用开台灯也能看清楚。
快把今天记进登记本：老陈夸了一张打印纸！
老板，别高兴得太早。下雨的时候，还是纸本子赢。
快看院子里的挂钟——五点半了！我们去点灯笼吧！
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
这块木板在我手里十五年，一直只有一到八号挂钩。

'For fifteen years in my hands, this wooden board only ever held hooks one through eight.' "Yizhi", literally "one straight line", captures something staying the same the whole time. And "guagou" pairs "hang" with "hook" so there is never any doubt what kind of hook you mean.
您看右边——清漆下面本来就有两个小小的螺丝孔。

'Look on the right edge—there were two tiny screw holes under the varnish all along.' Chen uses respectful "nin" with his boss, and "benlai jiu you" is a natural everyday chunk meaning "it was already there from the very start".
不会吧！三十年前，九号挂钩就挂在那儿！
'No way! Thirty years ago, hook number nine hung right there!' "Buhui ba!" literally asks "Couldn't be, right?"—one of Mandarin's most common ways to say "No way!" in happy surprise.
转一圈，转两圈……结实的黄铜九号挂钩，回家了。

'One turn, two turns... solid brass hook number nine, back home where it belongs.' Where English counts "one turn", Chen puts the action first: "turn one circle, turn two circles". Notice "huangtong" for brass—literally "yellow copper".
老陈，我可以亲手把阳光房的大钥匙挂上去吗？
'May I hang the big sunroom key up on it myself, Chen?' "Qinshou" joins "one's own" and "hand" for doing something meaningful yourself, while "gua shangqu" traces the key going up onto the board.
挂吧，小晴。这个星期你辛苦了。

'Go right ahead, Qing. You earned it with all your hard work this week.' "Ni xinku le", word for word "you tasted bitter toil", is how Mandarin speakers warmly thank a colleague for real effort—coming from Chen, that is gold.
等等——老陈，你账本里夹着的那张塑封卡片是什么？

'Wait—Chen, what is that laminated card tucked inside your paper ledger?' "Jia" means holding something pinched between two surfaces, whether pages of a ledger or a pair of chopsticks, and "sufeng" literally says "plastic-sealed".
哈！老陈，你偷偷留了一份我打印的咖啡馆菜单？！

'Aha! Did you secretly keep a copy of my printed café menu, Chen?!' Doubling "steal" into "toutou" drops any crime and playfully means "on the sly". Notice "fen", the counter Mandarin uses for copies of menus, newspapers, or portions.
只是因为你的大数字不用开台灯也能看清楚。

'Only because your big numbers are easy to read clearly without turning on a lamp.' In Mandarin you "open" a lamp—"kai taideng"—rather than switching it on, and "buyong", literally "no need to use", means "without having to".
快把今天记进登记本：老陈夸了一张打印纸！

'Write this day down in the guest book: Chen praised a printed page!' Flat thin items like sheets of paper, cards, and tabletops all take the counter "zhang", originally a word for stretching a bowstring wide.
老板，别高兴得太早。下雨的时候，还是纸本子赢。
'Don't celebrate too much, boss. When it rains, paper books still win.' "Bie gaoxing de tai zao"—literally "don't be happy too early"—is the crisp everyday twin of "don't celebrate too soon".
快看院子里的挂钟——五点半了！我们去点灯笼吧！

'Look at the courtyard clock—half past five! Let us go light the lanterns!' Notice "dian" doing double duty in one breath: first "five o'clock" in "wu dian ban", and then "light the lanterns" in "dian denglong", from touching a tiny point of flame to a wick.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.
这块木板在我手里十五年，一直只有一到八号挂钩。
您看右边——清漆下面本来就有两个小小的螺丝孔。
不会吧！三十年前，九号挂钩就挂在那儿！

哈！老陈，你偷偷留了一份我打印的咖啡馆菜单？！
只是因为你的大数字不用开台灯也能看清楚。
快把今天记进登记本：老陈夸了一张打印纸！
老板，别高兴得太早。下雨的时候，还是纸本子赢。
快看院子里的挂钟——五点半了！我们去点灯笼吧！
The brass hook number nine is back on the wooden board, and even Chen keeps Qing's printed menu tucked in his ledger. See you next time.
回头见！
